title: How fast the Board says yes, by department
question: How many days pass between the introduction of a contract, grant, lease or settlement file and the Board’s final vote, and which departments’ files move faster or slower than like files?
finding: 2,326 such files introduced from July 2018 to 2026 reached a final vote; the typical one took 35 days, and 75% took between three and seven weeks. 92% had exactly one committee hearing. By kind the middle value is 35 days for a contract, 35 days for a grant the City accepts, 42 days for a lease or property, 35 days for a grant agreement, 49 days for a settlement, 21 days for a loan; by calendar year of introduction it runs from 28 to 49 days. Against like files, the quickest departments are Real Estate Division (-10 days over 186 files); Mayor's Office (-8 days over 49 files); Treasure Island Development Authority (-5 days over 17 files); and the slowest Fire (+29 days over 19); Children, Youth and Their Families (+27 days over 25); Public Works (+22 days over 48). 2 of the 29 departments are faster, and 5 slower, than random sets of files of the same size would be 95% of the time (faster: Real Estate Division; Mayor's Office) (slower: Fire; Children, Youth and Their Families; Public Works; Police; Recreation and Park); chance alone would put one or two of 29 outside that range, so some departments’ files do move at their own pace.
how: Files are the Board’s contract, agreement, grant, lease, loan and settlement files introduced on or after 1 July 2018, with the action history from the Board’s legislation site. Days run from the date of introduction to the Board’s own final vote ("adopted" for a resolution, "finally passed" for an ordinance), not to the Mayor’s signature. Each file is set against like files: the same kind, the same type of legislation, the same size band and the same calendar year of introduction, widened to kind and year when fewer than six files match. "Against like files" is the average difference in days; negative is faster. Departments with fewer than 12 timed files are left out. The last column marks a department whose average lies outside the range that 1,000 random sets of the same number of timed files fall in 95% of the time. Ranked fastest first.
limits: Times fall in steps of seven days, as the Board’s meetings do, and three weeks is close to the floor for a file that goes to committee. Speed depends mostly on the calendar and the committee: a file introduced just before a break in the meetings waits, and an ordinance is voted twice ("passed on first reading", then "finally passed"). A fast file is not a favoured one: complete paperwork and an uncontested renewal pass quickly too. The department is read from the wording of the title. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
